title: I built and shipped Majestic Gems using generative AI for coding, UI, assets, VFX, and iteration — here’s what actually worked
author: owais6153
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I recently released **Majestic Gems**, a casual gem merge/shooter game for Android, and most of the development workflow relied heavily on generative AI.

What interested me most during development wasn’t just “can AI generate code?”  it was whether AI could actually help me move through the full game-development loop: mechanics, debugging, UI, balancing, assets, VFX, analytics, and production.

For the coding side, I used AI coding agents to help build and iterate on the Godot project. I still had to define the mechanics very precisely, because vague prompts caused some pretty bad regressions. One example was the merge system: I needed gems to merge **only when they physically touched**, while also keeping the physics predictable around walls and the board boundaries. The more specific the gameplay rules became, the better the agent performed.

AI was also heavily involved in the visual direction. I iterated through a lot of styles before settling on the current purple/gold fantasy gem theme. Generative image tools helped with things such as:

* UI panels and buttons
* Power-up icons
* Daily mission icons
* Treasure chest states
* Special striped gems
* Background concepts
* VFX concepts for merges, bombs, magnets, shuffling, etc.
* Store/marketing artwork

One thing I learned pretty quickly is that **AI-generated assets are much easier to use when you establish a visual family first**. Early on, I kept asking for individual assets and they looked like they belonged to different games. Once I started using the same gem shapes, materials, purple/gold UI language, lighting, and proportions as references, consistency improved a lot.

The same happened with coding. Giving an agent a broad request like “make merges more satisfying” usually produced questionable results. Giving it something closer to:

“Keep the existing physics unchanged, add a short impact scale pulse, spawn 1–3 miniature gem particles, add a ring VFX, escalate pitch for consecutive merges, and don’t remove the original gem before the merge transition finishes”

worked much better.

AI also helped me with things outside the obvious areas:

* creating and fixing Firebase analytics events
* reviewing ad integration
* balancing limited-shot levels
* designing coin sinks and powers
* improving onboarding/retention ideas
* generating store creatives
* reviewing gameplay footage and identifying UX problems

The biggest limitation I’ve noticed is that AI can move extremely fast in the **wrong direction** if the constraints aren’t explicit. For a game, that can mean changing physics, introducing inconsistent art, overdesigning UI, or adding systems that technically work but don’t feel good.

So my workflow became much more iterative:

**prototype → test on device → record gameplay → critique → give AI a very narrow correction → test again**

That worked much better than asking an agent to “finish the game.”

The game is now live on Android, and I’m still improving it.

**Majestic Gems:**  
[Google Play Store Link](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.owais.majestygems)

I’d be really interested to hear how other people here are using generative AI in actual game production rather than just prototyping.

I’m happy to share more about the prompts/workflow I used if anyone is interested.
